description: One Student. One Mission. One Man Orbit. TO THE MOON!
summary:
EMBER (Explainable Microgravity Burn Evidence & Regime-Bridging) is an interactive research platform that helps researchers investigate microgravity combustion by connecting user-specified fire conditions with traceable NASA experimental records and published physics models.

EMBER integrates NASA’s BASS-II experimental archive, source-aware evidence retrieval, mathematical combustion analysis, and constrained regime-bridging methods. Its Physics Model Router selects material- and geometry-specific formulations, while its Evidence Explorer displays relevant experimental conditions, observations, and source references. A separate Bayesian model provides limited-scope analysis of sustained ignition in audited PMMA-rod experiments.

Crucially, EMBER distinguishes observed evidence from calculated quantities and model estimates. When available evidence or model applicability is insufficient, the platform explicitly abstains instead of presenting unsupported predictions.

EMBER aims to make existing spacecraft fire research more accessible, explainable, and scientifically transparent—not replace physical experimentation or certify spacecraft materials as safe.

This is not a NASA endorsement, certification, or independently peer-reviewed manuscript.

Abstract

EMBER is a source-aware combustion research prototype that connects user-entered conditions to NASA microgravity fire experiments and published, family-specific physical scaling relationships. Its architecture combines an audited metadata/evidence store based on NASA BASS-II (PSI-25), record reconciliation with NASA/TM-20210011385, gated condition-similarity retrieval, a six-family physics-model router, constrained inverse-design methods, uncertainty-aware model infrastructure, and explicit scientific abstention. The application prioritizes provenance: recorded experimental observations are distinguished from literature-domain anchors, physics-derived quantities, Bayesian statistical estimates, and proposed analogue conditions. At the checked deployment, 129 PSI experimental-table metadata rows are ingested, 126 appendix test identifiers are reconciled, 47 records have separate report-table links, and five unresolved NASA source-field discrepancies are quarantined. A narrow empirical Bayesian logistic model uses 19 audited PMMA-rod observations (16 positives, three negatives); its reported leave-one-out ROC AUC is 0.9792, Brier score 0.0696, and log loss 0.2429, without external validation or a justified F1 statistic. This document describes the scientific workflow, governing mathematical expressions, assumptions, software components, test cases, research value, and outstanding validation work. EMBER does not claim universal flame prediction, complete cross-gravity equivalence, or spacecraft material safety certification.

Index Terms—microgravity combustion, BASS-II, NASA PSI, evidence retrieval, physical similitude, regime bridging, inverse design, Bayesian modeling, scientific abstention.

I.  Introduction

Fire behavior changes when buoyancy, forced convection, oxygen concentration, ambient pressure, material composition, and specimen geometry change. Results from Earth-normal-gravity screening cannot automatically be transferred to spacecraft or reduced-gravity environments. NASA’s BASS-II investigation examined solid-fuel ignition, flame growth, spread, and extinction in controlled low-velocity flows aboard the ISS [1], [2]. Complementary NASA-supported investigations developed limited-range physical relationships linking mixed convection, pressure and gravity in particular combustible materials [3]–[8].

The engineering challenge is not simply to retrieve a paper: a researcher must identify a comparable experiment, distinguish observed conditions from model assumptions, reproduce a relevant physics relation, judge its domain of applicability, and explain when no justified correspondence exists. EMBER makes this reasoning workflow inspectable in one web application. The project supports NASA Space Apps’ Flame in Freefall theme by promoting usable, traceable scientific evidence rather than implying that a single AI model can simulate arbitrary fires.

II.  Objectives and Research Questions

  • Provide an accessible NASA BASS-II evidence explorer with experiment IDs, source links, field-level provenance, and preserved unknowns.
  • Compute interpretable, material-specific combustion quantities only when a literature-supported adapter applies.
  • Find bounded analogue/regime conditions by matching an explicitly named physical quantity; disclose mismatches in other dimensions.
  • Present statistical estimates separately from deterministic model results, with sample size and uncertainty.
  • Refuse unsupported conclusions with identifiable abstention statuses, missing-evidence explanations, and reproducible input examples.

Research questions: (RQ1) Can heterogeneous NASA fire records be reconciled into retrievable, source-traceable entries without inventing missing measurements? (RQ2) Can the system execute published family-specific scaling formulae while maintaining model-domain controls? (RQ3) Can bounded inverse design identify a numerical similitude match without misrepresenting it as complete physical equivalence? (RQ4) Can narrow statistical model outputs be reported without overstating external validity?

III.  Literature and Scientific Foundation

A.  NASA BASS-II experimental evidence

The NASA PSI-25 Version 4 archive is an ISS microgravity investigation released under CC0-1.0; the public archive reports 694 file listings and metadata for experiment-table records [1]. The BASS-II Summary Report documents a small flow duct, astronaut-controlled ignition and fan settings, recorded video/still imagery, oxygen/CO/CO₂ measurement, and tests that varied fuel, geometry, oxygen and flow [2]. Neither archive file totals nor interface display rows equal a count of independently validated measured flame outcomes.

B.  Pressure–gravity similitude for thick PMMA

Thomsen and colleagues examined concurrent flame spread over 10-mm PMMA under approximately 40–100 kPa normal-gravity conditions at 0.20 m/s, compared with Saffire microgravity evidence [3]. The derivation relates a mixed-convection velocity to pressure, gravity and pyrolysis length. Matching this quantity can suggest a partial analogue, but pressure also changes oxygen partial pressure and gas-phase chemistry; therefore, a match is not full fire equivalence.

C.  PMMA rod blowoff/stretch research

Marcum, Ferkul and Olson compared normal-gravity PMMA rod blowoff limits and ISS BASS-II rod behavior, accounting for blockage, a rod-size correction and buoyancy-related stretch [4]. This is a rod-specific relation; neither an oxygen-only ignition probability nor a universal multi-material combustion model follows from it.

D.  Other evidence-backed model families

SIBAL mixed-convection work investigated 75% cotton/25% fiberglass composite fabric and pressure-lowered Earth tests compared with microgravity conditions [5]. NASA Kimwipes studies developed regression relationships for specific microgravity flame-spread protocols [6]. Thin PMMA Narrow Channel Apparatus (NCA) investigations treated channel confinement as a microgravity analogue under defined specimen/gap conditions [7]. Published electrical-wire research explored a conditional low-pressure, partial-gravity similarity under quiescent conditions [8]. Reduced-gravity oxygen-threshold lookup for selected materials must preserve the source-specific pressure, duration and test criteria [9].

E.  Design gap and contribution

Existing publications provide experiments or constrained physical equations, but not a single universal conversion rule. EMBER’s contribution is an integrated evidence-to-model workflow: structured NASA ingestion, source-grounded retrieval, explicit model routing, bounded numerical matching, calibrated statistical context when available, visible limitations, and abstention. The contribution is the transparent integration, not a newly discovered fundamental combustion law.

IV.  System Architecture and Processing Pipeline

Fig. 1. System Architecture


Fig. 2. EMBER research pipeline.

Stage 1 — Data acquisition: NASA PSI-25 source metadata, raw-file listing, linked BASS-II technical report appendix and supporting research references are registered with URLs and version identifiers. Stage 2 — Data engineering: records are normalized, reconciled and quality-flagged without erasing disagreements. Stage 3 — Evidence retrieval: material/family eligibility and numerical/categorical similarity identify relevant source conditions. Stage 4 — Model routing: geometry-specific applicability rules select an appropriate physics adapter or refuse a model. Stage 5 — Reporting: quantitative fingerprints, source links, residuals, warnings, and abstention statuses are returned to interactive panels and exports.

Mathematical and Algorithmic Layer of EMBER

1. k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) and Weighted Gower Similarity

EMBER employs a condition-aware evidence-retrieval approach to identify NASA combustion experiments relevant to user-specified environmental and material conditions.

Unlike conventional classification, EMBER's kNN-style retrieval identifies similar experimental records without assigning fabricated combustion outcomes.

1.1 Experimental Feature Representation

Each combustion scenario is represented by a feature vector:

x = [M, G, O₂, P, U, r, L]

Where:

  • M: Material classification
  • G: Specimen geometry
  • O₂: Oxygen concentration
  • P: Ambient pressure
  • U: Airflow velocity
  • r: Specimen radius, when applicable
  • L: Relevant specimen or pyrolysis length

The NASA experimental repository contains both numerical and categorical variables. Therefore, EMBER employs a weighted Gower-style similarity measure to compare experimental conditions across different feature types.

1.2 Weighted Gower Similarity

The generalized similarity function is:

S(i,j) = [Σₖ₌₁ᵖ wₖ · δᵢⱼₖ · sᵢⱼₖ] / [Σₖ₌₁ᵖ wₖ · δᵢⱼₖ]

Where:

  • S(i,j): Overall similarity between scenarios i and j
  • wₖ: Weight assigned to feature k
  • δᵢⱼₖ: Indicator specifying whether feature k can be compared
  • sᵢⱼₖ: Similarity of feature k between scenarios i and j
  • p: Total number of considered features

The similarity function considers only comparable attributes, preventing missing experimental fields from being treated as confirmed values.

Numerical Feature Similarity

For numerical attributes, a conventional Gower similarity component is calculated as:

sᵢⱼₖ = 1 − |xᵢₖ − xⱼₖ| / Rₖ

Where:

  • xᵢₖ: Value of feature k in scenario i
  • xⱼₖ: Value of feature k in scenario j
  • Rₖ: Normalization range associated with feature k

The numerical similarity is bounded to the interval [0, 1] where necessary.

Categorical Feature Similarity

Categorical attributes are compared using:

sᵢⱼₖ = 1, if the attributes match

sᵢⱼₖ = 0, otherwise

EMBER additionally applies material- and geometry-aware eligibility restrictions to prevent experimentally unrelated fuels or specimens from being treated as physically equivalent merely because their environmental variables are similar.

The exact feature weights and normalization ranges must remain consistent with the implemented retrieval configuration.

1.3 kNN-Style Evidence Retrieval

After calculating similarity values, EMBER ranks eligible NASA experiments and retrieves the k most relevant records.

Algorithm 1: Condition-Aware NASA Evidence Retrieval

Input:

  • User-defined combustion scenario X
  • NASA experimental repository D
  • Number of nearest records k

Procedure:

  1. Validate the user-provided combustion parameters.
  2. Identify experimental records eligible for comparison.
    • Identify comparable numerical and categorical attributes.
    • Normalize numerical feature differences.
    • Calculate individual feature similarities.
    • Apply configured similarity weights.
    • Calculate the weighted Gower similarity.
    • Preserve missing-data and source-quality flags.
  3. Rank records according to their calculated similarity values.
  4. Select the k highest-ranking eligible records.
  5. Attach the corresponding NASA experiment identifier, original source, experimental conditions, and provenance information.
  6. Return the ranked experimental evidence to the NASA Evidence Explorer.

Output:

A ranked collection of source-linked NASA combustion experiments.

Scientific Interpretation

The similarity score represents the degree of similarity between documented experimental conditions. It does not represent ignition probability, predictive confidence, or proof that two experiments exhibit identical combustion behavior.

2. Bayesian Logistic Regression for Ignition Analysis

EMBER incorporates a separate Bayesian statistical model for investigating sustained-ignition observations associated with a specific NASA BASS-II PMMA-rod experimental protocol.

The audited dataset contains:

  • 19 source-normalized observations
  • 16 positive observations
  • 3 negative observations

The model uses calibrated initial oxygen concentration as its explanatory variable.

2.1 Logistic Probability Function

The probability of a positive sustained-ignition observation is represented by:

P(y = 1 | O₂, β) = 1 / [1 + exp(−(β₀ + β₁ · O₂))]

Where:

  • P(y = 1 | O₂, β): Probability of a positive observation under the defined experimental protocol
  • y: Binary observed outcome
  • O₂: Initial oxygen concentration
  • β₀: Logistic regression intercept
  • β₁: Oxygen-associated regression coefficient
  • exp: Exponential function

The logistic function maps the linear predictor to a probability between zero and one.

2.2 Bayesian Posterior Inference

Unlike conventional logistic regression, which may estimate a single coefficient vector, Bayesian logistic regression represents uncertainty over model parameters.

Bayes' theorem is expressed as:

p(β | D) = [p(D | β) · p(β)] / p(D)

Where:

  • β: Model parameter vector
  • D: Observed experimental dataset
  • p(β | D): Posterior parameter distribution
  • p(D | β): Likelihood of observed data given the parameters
  • p(β): Prior distribution
  • p(D): Marginal likelihood

The documented implementation constrains the oxygen-associated slope to nonnegative values using a positive-support prior.

This reflects the model's assumed nondecreasing relationship between oxygen concentration and sustained ignition within its defined experimental scope.

2.3 Posterior Predictive Probability

The posterior predictive probability integrates over uncertainty in the regression coefficients:

P(y = 1 | O₂, D) = ∫ P(y* = 1 | O₂*, β) · p(β | D) dβ**

Where:

  • y:* Outcome for a new experimental condition
  • O₂:* New oxygen concentration
  • D: Existing experimental observations
  • β: Bayesian regression parameters

This formulation accounts for uncertainty in the estimated relationship rather than relying exclusively on a single coefficient estimate.

2.4 Quantitative Model Evaluation

The previously documented production calibration reports the following leave-one-out cross-validation diagnostics:

Evaluation Metric

Reported Value

ROC AUC

0.9792

Brier Score

0.0696

Log Loss

0.2429

These values describe different statistical properties and must not be combined into an overall accuracy percentage.

Brier Score

The Brier score evaluates the mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and binary observations.

BS = (1/N) · Σᵢ₌₁ᴺ (pᵢ − yᵢ)²

Where:

  • N: Number of evaluated observations
  • pᵢ: Predicted probability for observation i
  • yᵢ: Actual binary observation

Lower Brier scores indicate smaller probability-prediction errors.

Logarithmic Loss

Logarithmic loss evaluates probabilistic prediction performance while penalizing confident incorrect predictions.

LL = −(1/N) · Σᵢ₌₁ᴺ [yᵢ · ln(pᵢ) + (1 − yᵢ) · ln(1 − pᵢ)]

Where:

  • ln: Natural logarithm
  • pᵢ: Predicted probability
  • yᵢ: Actual observation

Lower logarithmic loss indicates better probabilistic performance.

Precision, Recall, and F1-Score

For completeness, the conventional classification metrics are:

Precision = TP / (TP + FP)

Recall = TP / (TP + FN)

F1 = 2 · Precision · Recall / (Precision + Recall)

Where:

  • TP: True positives
  • FP: False positives
  • FN: False negatives

However, an experimentally defensible F1-score cannot currently be reported without a specified classification threshold, verified fold-level predictions, and the corresponding confusion matrix.

Scientific Limitation

The model contains only three negative observations. Consequently, the reported ROC AUC must be interpreted cautiously.

Moreover, the model is an ISS BASS-II protocol-specific statistical reference. It is not a general-purpose ignition predictor for arbitrary terrestrial, lunar, Martian, or spacecraft conditions.

3. Physics-Aware Combustion Regime Bridging

EMBER incorporates material-specific mathematical formulations to investigate relationships between combustion conditions under different gravitational, pressure, and airflow environments.

Rather than relying on one universal combustion equation, EMBER uses a physics-model router that identifies applicable formulations according to the material, specimen geometry, and supported experimental domain.

3.1 Mixed-Convection Model

For thick PMMA, the documented mixed-convection relationship uses the Froude number to describe the relative importance of imposed flow and gravitational acceleration.

The Froude number is:

Fr = U_f² / (g · Lₚ)

Where:

  • Fr: Froude number
  • U_f: Forced airflow velocity
  • g: Gravitational acceleration
  • Lₚ: Pyrolysis length

The equivalent mixed-convection velocity is expressed as:

Uₘ = U_f · (P / P₀) · [1 + (g · Lₚ / U_f²)²]^(¼)

Where:

  • Uₘ: Equivalent mixed-convection velocity
  • U_f: Imposed airflow velocity
  • P: Ambient pressure
  • P₀: Reference pressure
  • g: Gravitational acceleration
  • Lₚ: Pyrolysis length

This mathematical relationship combines pressure scaling and gravity-dependent convection effects to characterize a particular model quantity.

A near-zero difference in equivalent mixed-convection velocity does not establish identical ignition behavior, flame-spread rates, or extinction limits.

3.2 PMMA Rod Total-Stretch Model

The PMMA-rod physics adapter evaluates the combined influence of forced convection and buoyancy-related stretch.

Raw Forced Stretch

The unadjusted forced stretch is:

a_raw = (3 · U) / (2 · r)

Where:

  • a_raw: Raw forced stretch rate
  • U: Forced airflow velocity
  • r: Rod radius

Blockage Correction

The blockage factor accounts for the reduction in available flow area caused by the rod.

B = A_tube / (A_tube − A_rod)

Where:

  • B: Blockage correction factor
  • A_tube: Cross-sectional area of the surrounding flow passage
  • A_rod: Cross-sectional area of the rod

Adjusted Forced Stretch

The adjusted forced-stretch relationship is:

a_forced = a_raw · B · √(r / r₀)

Where:

  • a_forced: Adjusted forced stretch
  • a_raw: Raw forced stretch
  • B: Blockage factor
  • r: Rod radius
  • r₀: Reference rod radius

Buoyant Stretch

The gravitational contribution is represented by:

a_buoyant = K · √(g / r)

Where:

  • a_buoyant: Buoyancy-associated stretch contribution
  • K: Source-specific empirical coefficient
  • g: Gravitational acceleration
  • r: Rod radius

The coefficient and input units must follow the original empirical model.

Total Stretch

The total calculated stretch is:

a_total = a_forced + a_buoyant

Where:

  • a_total: Total stretch rate
  • a_forced: Adjusted forced-stretch component
  • a_buoyant: Buoyancy-associated contribution

The resulting stretch rate is expressed in s⁻¹.

Scientific Interpretation

The calculated total stretch represents a particular physical quantity within the PMMA-rod model.

It should not be interpreted directly as an observed blowoff velocity, flame-spread measurement, ignition probability, or independently validated fire-equivalence prediction.

3.3 Constrained Inverse Design and Regime Bridging

EMBER's inverse-design component searches for alternative experimental configurations that approximate a selected physics quantity while respecting model applicability restrictions.

A generalized optimization objective is:

x = argmin₍ₓ∈Ω₎ [D(Φ(x), Φ(xₜ)) + λ · C(x)]*

Where:

  • x:* Optimal proposed comparison scenario
  • xₜ: Target experimental scenario
  • Ω: Feasible domain of candidate conditions
  • Φ(x): Selected physics fingerprint
  • D: Mathematical discrepancy between fingerprints
  • λ: Penalty weighting coefficient
  • C(x): Constraint or extrapolation penalty

The optimization aims to minimize differences between selected physical quantities under explicitly defined constraints.

For example, EMBER's PMMA-rod adapter may search for conditions that approximately match total stretch between different environmental configurations.

However, matching total stretch alone does not demonstrate equivalence in flame chemistry, thermal radiation, oxygen transport, ignition history, or material response.

Regime bridging is therefore interpreted as a bounded mathematical comparison, not universal combustion equivalence.

4. Scientific Abstention and Model Applicability

A defining feature of EMBER is its integration of scientific constraints into the computational workflow.

Before reporting a calculated physics result, the application evaluates whether the requested scenario lies within the selected model's supported domain.

4.1 Model Applicability Assessment

Model applicability depends on the compatibility of the user-defined scenario with the physical model's assumptions.

The relevant checks include:

  • Material classification
  • Specimen geometry
  • Oxygen concentration
  • Ambient pressure
  • Gravitational environment
  • Forced airflow velocity
  • Required specimen dimensions
  • Availability and interpretation of supporting scientific references

4.2 Scientific Abstention Procedure

Algorithm 2: Scientific Model Applicability and Abstention

Input:

  • User-defined combustion scenario X
  • Available physics-model registry M
  • Supporting scientific repository D

Procedure:

  1. Validate all user inputs and physical units.
  2. Identify the material and specimen geometry.
  3. Determine whether a corresponding physics adapter exists.
  4. Retrieve the adapter's supported experimental domain.
  5. Evaluate the input conditions against the model's applicability restrictions.
  6. If the input violates the supported domain, return OUT_OF_DOMAIN_ABSTENTION.
  7. Otherwise, compute the model-specific physics fingerprint.
  8. Identify admissible comparison conditions for regime bridging.
  9. Evaluate the selected physical quantity and numerical residual.
  10. If no justified comparison is available, return NO_VALIDATED_BRIDGE.
  11. Otherwise, return the calculated quantity and its scientific explanation.
  12. Attach model assumptions, source references, applicable restrictions, and unresolved limitations.

Output:

A bounded scientific result or an explicit abstention status.

4.3 Scientific Abstention Categories

OUT_OF_DOMAIN_ABSTENTION

This status indicates that the selected physical model does not support the requested input conditions.

The system must not manufacture a model-derived prediction outside its authorized scientific domain.

NO_VALIDATED_BRIDGE

This status indicates that the model may evaluate a physical quantity, but no scientifically justified comparison is available under the selected regime-bridging constraints.

The absence of a supported bridge does not necessarily mean that no NASA experiment exists for similar conditions.

4.4 Scientific Integrity

EMBER distinguishes among:

  • Experimentally observed NASA evidence
  • Source-linked experimental metadata
  • Mathematical quantities derived from physical models
  • Separate Bayesian statistical estimates
  • Proposed regime-bridging conditions
  • Unsupported or out-of-domain scenarios

This separation reduces the risk of presenting mathematical extrapolation as experimentally verified combustion behavior.

EMBER combines evidence retrieval, physical modeling, statistical inference, and scientific applicability controls within a unified computational workflow.

The system follows five primary stages.

Stage 1 — Experimental Condition Acquisition

The user specifies material properties and environmental conditions, including gravity, pressure, oxygen concentration, airflow velocity, and specimen geometry.

The system validates these parameters before initiating scientific analysis.

Stage 2 — NASA Evidence Retrieval

EMBER evaluates relevant records using condition-aware Gower similarity and kNN-style retrieval.

Eligible records are ranked according to their similarity and linked to their original NASA sources.

Stage 3 — Physics-Based Analysis

The physics-model router identifies the corresponding material- and geometry-specific model.

Depending on applicability, EMBER computes supported quantities such as equivalent mixed-convection velocity, PMMA-rod total stretch, or model-specific empirical quantities.

Stage 4 — Physics Regime Bridging

When scientifically applicable, EMBER uses constrained inverse-design calculations to investigate alternative conditions that approximate a selected physical quantity.

Any successful comparison is restricted to the quantity and model assumptions being evaluated.

A separate Bayesian ignition reference may provide limited statistical context where its original experimental protocol applies. It does not automatically become a prediction for the physics scenario.

Stage 5 — Explainability and Scientific Abstention

The final output presents:

V.  NASA Data Engineering and Provenance Methodology

A.  Original NASA sources and ingestion

The official NASA PSI-25 Version 4 archive [1] is the primary machine-readable source. The BASS-II 2021 technical memorandum [2] supplies independent appendix test IDs, experimental notes and table-level source context. EMBER’s production audit records a 16,590-byte source experimental CSV and SHA-256 checksum 71e792bf6b5fb5ea620c5dd70fbbac05515992e12aefcf5dff47312caa48c042. The corresponding NASA report and metadata manifests have separate stored hashes. These hashes support provenance integrity checks; they do not prove the physical accuracy of instrument readings.

B.  Normalization, join keys and source reconciliation

  • Parse and retain raw NASA identifier, investigator/substudy, fuel label, geometry, oxygen, flow sequence and source file descriptors.
  • Normalize numeric units only when the source label and unit interpretation are known. Keep source value, parsed value, and transformation or uncertainty note.
  • Reconcile PSI experiment identifiers against Appendix A’s 126 as-run tests; preserve original historical and repeat-test scope.
  • Join to published report tables/appendix observations using exact IDs and evidence-backed mapping; do not add repeated source descriptions as new independent experiments.
  • Preserve calibrated initial/final O₂ as separate variables from raw sensor readings. Do not infer O₂ at each fan plateau from run-level endpoints.
  • Represent missing, not-recorded, instrument-failed and contradictory values as distinct machine-readable states.
  • Attach source URL, report/page/table, quality-verification class, verification action and unresolved QA flags to each record.

The live reconciliation identifies 129 PSI metadata rows, 126 report Appendix A IDs and three 2016-dated CSV-only IDs (O20, O21, O22). The public website’s apparent 130-item display was reproduced as a parser artifact involving a trailing empty line, not 130 authenticated independent tests. The NASA report’s 126 appendix runs and the 129 metadata rows are different denominators and should not be added together.

C.  Quality assurance and conflict quarantine

The checked V5 production audit reports 756 gas-field comparisons with five unresolved CSV–report disagreements. Rather than silently replacing NASA values, EMBER marks disputed values as unresolved and excludes them from supported numeric conclusions. A review of identifiers, gas columns and notes across 11 appendix pages does not constitute complete certification of all NASA assets or all Tables 5.1/7.1 entries.

D.  Media and frame-screening controls

NASA PSI lists experimental MP4 assets; live EMBER screening currently reports eight previously byte-verified media files, five MP4s processed through a full-frame computational visual screening path, and 7,237 decoded frames in that path. No independent video ignition/extinction event labels or spread-rate measurements are certified. Image intensity and frame difference may guide inspection but are not flame-event ground truth. The frame-screened clips and byte-verified sets can overlap and must not be added into a false distinct-video total.

VI.  Evidence Retrieval and Mathematical Similarity

For a user scenario x and candidate source record z, EMBER first enforces material/family eligibility. Within the eligible pool it uses weighted Gower-style mixed-type similarity, excluding missing fields rather than imputing them. A generic form is:

S(x,z) = [Σⱼ wⱼ δⱼ sⱼ(x,z)] / [Σⱼ wⱼ δⱼ]     (1)

where wⱼ is a feature weight, δⱼ indicates valid comparison availability, and sⱼ∈[0,1] is a categorical equality score or a normalized bounded numeric closeness score. A representative numerical comparison is sⱼ=max(0,1−|xⱼ−zⱼ|/Rⱼ) for a documented range Rⱼ; the deployed family-specific normalization and weights govern exact ranking. Missingness and the number of compared fields must be shown alongside the score.

This similarity ranks experimental conditions; it is NOT model confidence, a probability of identical flame behavior, a probability of ignition, or proof that an unrecorded outcome occurred. Original observed runs, source-condition anchors, calculated physical points, and proposed surrogate points carry separate provenance classes. The default application can present a small ranked shortlist, while the BASS-II archive supports independent test-ID search and original appendix navigation.

VII.  Physics Model Router and Governing Mathematics

The live /api/models registry identifies six adapters. The router selects a material/geometry family and checks input domain, including units, oxygen, pressure, flow, specimen and physical source constraints. A valid numerical expression without corresponding domain evidence is not automatically an IN_DOMAIN experimental prediction.

NCA gap / material / flow constraints; not direct g conversion

A.  Thick-PMMA concurrent mixed-convection adapter

Define U_f as imposed gas velocity (m s⁻¹), P as total gas pressure (kPa), P₀=101.325 kPa, g as absolute gravitational acceleration (m s⁻²), and ℓ_p as pyrolysis length (m). The Froude form and the source-derived equivalent mixed velocity are [3]:

Fr = U_f² / (g ℓ_p)     (2)

U_m = U_f (P/P₀) [1 + (g ℓ_p/U_f²)²]^(1/4)     (3)

At g=0, the Froude-number expression has a singular limit but U_m has the finite zero-gravity limit U_f(P/P₀). The implementation guards exact-zero arithmetic instead of emitting nonfinite JSON. When searching Earth-1g analogues, EMBER attempts to match U_m using source-restricted pressure/flow choices and reports changes in oxygen partial pressure and other unmatched physics.

B.  PMMA rod stagnation-flow stretch adapter

For rod radius r (cm) and imposed U (cm s⁻¹), the published model [4] uses forced stretch, blockage adjustment, normalized radius correction and buoyant stretch. Let A_tube be tube section and A_rod be rod cross-section; r₀ denotes the source baseline rod radius.

a_raw = (3/2) (U/r)     (4)

B = A_tube / (A_tube − A_rod)     (5)

a_forced = a_raw B √(r/r₀)     (6)

a_buoyant = K √(g/r),  K = 1.44  (source-specific)     (7)

a_total = a_forced + a_buoyant     (8)

The acceleration g and radius r must be in internally compatible cm/s² and cm for Eq. (7). All reported a terms have s⁻¹ units. K is a published PMMA-rod-specific correlation parameter, not an established universal constant across combustible materials. A computed stretch value is not itself an observed blowoff velocity, safe oxygen limit, ignition probability, or empirically validated cross-gravity match.

C.  SIBAL concurrent flame-spread family

EMBER includes a SIBAL cotton/fiberglass mixed-convection model rooted in published limited-condition normal-g versus microgravity research [5]. Here the relevant heat-transfer scaling depends on the physical pyrolysis length, ambient pressure, gravity, forced flow, and constrained material dimensions. It is not legitimate to replace pyrolysis length with overall sample length without the source-specific definition, nor to call arbitrary oxygen/flow combinations experimentally verified.

D.  Kimwipes microgravity empirical family

The Kimwipes family implements a NASA-source empirical spread-rate relation for selected thin cellulose-fuel conditions [6]. A recovered model-audit expression uses x = χ_O₂·U_(cm/s)·√(P/P₀), followed by v_(cm/s) = 0.2498x + 0.4038. This is an implementation-level regression representation; the exact input normalization, coefficient applicability and published experimental envelope should be reviewed at source before quantitative reuse. The system must suppress unsupported Earth/Moon/Mars transfer of a microgravity-only empirical law.

E.  LDPE insulated-wire and narrow-channel analogy

The LDPE wire family examines a conditional pressure–gravity similarity indicator proportional to P²g under specific low-pressure quiescent-wire conditions [8]. Because P²g alone does not enforce thermochemical or heat-loss equivalence, the output is a partial similitude criterion rather than a universal fire-spread rate. The thin-PMMA NCA adapter instead represents a restricted laboratory apparatus analogy: channel confinement suppresses buoyancy in defined gaps, flows and fuel thicknesses [7]. The NCA result should not be marketed as a numerical 1g-to-lunar-g conversion.

F.  Reduced-gravity material threshold evidence

Source-reported maximum oxygen concentration (MOC) and upward limiting oxygen index (ULOI) for Mylar G, Ultem 1000 and Nomex are kept as contextual observations [9]. Different material and gravity tests used distinct pressures, durations and criteria; raw lookup entries are not interpolated into universal safety thresholds.

VIII.  Constrained Physics Regime Bridging and Inverse Design

The goal of constrained inverse design is to find a candidate z in a physically and experimentally supported feasible domain Ω that matches one chosen scalar or limited-dimensional fingerprint Φ(x) of a target x. The generic mathematical form is:

z* = argmin_(z∈Ω) [D(Φ(z),Φ(x)) + λ·Penalty_extrap(z)]     (9)

Model-specific objectives are used: thick PMMA matches U_m; rod analysis matches a_total. The optimizer may return a proposed feasible analogue, an unmatched boundary, an extrapolation warning, or NO_VALIDATED_BRIDGE. User-fixed flow is treated as a constraint, not a suggestion. A near-zero numerical residual proves only algebraic agreement in the chosen reduced-order quantity, not identical combustion kinetics or flammability behavior.

A separate physically informative comparison is oxygen partial pressure p_O₂≈χ_O₂ P for an ideal-gas mixture. Even if the same O₂ mole fraction is entered, a change in total pressure changes p_O₂. Radiation, flame shape, thermal losses, transport, ignition history and material properties may remain unmatched. EMBER’s FireGap-style limitations must remain qualitative unless supported by actual measured coverage denominators.

p_O₂ = χ_O₂ · P     (10)

IX.  Bayesian Statistical Model and ML Readiness

A.  Audited empirical model

EMBER’s live calibration endpoint describes an oxygen-only Bayesian logistic regression for sustained ignition under a specified BASS-II Olson clear-PMMA-rod protocol. There are 19 source-normalized observations: 16 positives and 3 negatives. The feature is calibrated initial oxygen in percent, not gravity, pressure or material identity. The labels are based on an EMBER audit-normalization rule applied to published NASA observations; they are not NASA-issued calibrated probabilities.

Pr(y=1 | O₂, β) = 1 / [1 + exp{−(β₀ + β₁·O₂)}]     (11)

The slope coefficient is constrained β₁≥0 through a HalfNormal prior/support, enforcing a nondecreasing oxygen relationship. The source indicates deterministic two-dimensional quadrature for posterior calculations. A posterior predictive probability integrates the logistic response over posterior uncertainty, rather than relying only on one fitted coefficient vector:

Pr(y*=1|O₂*,D) = ∫ Pr(y*=1|O₂*,β) p(β|D) dβ     (12)

This is a small-sample empirical boundary model, not a general spaceship fire-risk score. It is deliberately separated from Earth-1g rod stretch and other geometry analyses. High apparent discrimination can arise in a narrowly ordered training set; repeated specimen dependence, prior choices and just three negatives limit confidence.

B.  Reported leave-one-out diagnostics

The deployed calibration endpoint currently reports leave-one-out ROC AUC 0.9791667, Brier score 0.0695761 and logarithmic loss 0.2428995. These are not independent held-out or external validation results. Without the per-fold predicted classes, a declared probability threshold and a complete confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1 and confidence intervals cannot be responsibly derived. A visually impressive but fabricated ROC curve, F1 value or confusion matrix would misrepresent the evidence.

Brier = (1/n) Σᵢ (pᵢ−yᵢ)²     (13)

LogLoss = −(1/n) Σᵢ [yᵢ ln pᵢ + (1−yᵢ) ln(1−pᵢ)]     (14)

F1 = 2·Precision·Recall / (Precision+Recall)     (15)

Fig. 5. Live self-reported leave-one-out metrics. Different definitions/directions apply; values are not combined into a single percentage or independent accuracy claim.

C.  Gaussian Process and Bayesian design infrastructure

The recovered scientific core documents an uncertainty-aware Matérn-5/2 Gaussian Process (GP) with white-noise kernel for future source-verified flame-spread outcome regression. The covariance family is:

k(r) = σ_f² [1 + √5r/ℓ + 5r²/(3ℓ²)] exp(−√5r/ℓ)     (16)

A provenance gate restricts training outcomes to explicitly verified observed data. The underlying research-core design includes an optional residual GP of the form y_obs=y_physics+δ_GP and candidate information-gain ranking. These capabilities must not be described as live, externally validated flame-spread models unless an appropriately sourced outcome calibration is actually available. In particular, the absence of adjudicated video labels blocks video-based supervised training.

IG_GP(x) = ½ ln[1 + σ_f²(x)/σ_n²]     (17)

A separate Bernoulli acquisition expression can prioritize oxygen levels for learning a calibrated binary boundary:

IG_Bern(x) = H(E[p_x]) − E[H(p_x)],  H(p)=−p ln p−(1−p)ln(1−p)     (18)

These are experiment-learning objectives, not a probability that a target spacecraft material is safe. The Gaussian-process information-gain infrastructure and the empirical Bayesian logistic ignition endpoint are distinct models with different training/readiness gates

X.  Explainability, Visualizations, and Scientific Abstention

EMBER’s interface is intended for a traceable review workflow rather than photorealistic fluid simulation. The NASA Evidence Explorer displays source-linked experiments and their observed or absent fields; the Physics Bridge displays model family, matched quantity, possible surrogate and residual; contextual readouts show oxygen, pressure, gravity and applicability; a gap/evidence panel distinguishes known and unresolved support. Schematic flame effects are user-interface illustrations rather than video evidence, CFD output or experimentally measured flame images.

XI.  Reproducible Scenarios and Illustrative Numerical Checks

A.  NASA BASS-II PMMA-rod evidence lookup

In the archive explorer, select investigator Olson and query O10. Record PSI25-O-O10 is a clear 1/4-inch PMMA rod. Its report-linked Appendix A.5 entry preserves calibrated initial O₂ 16.7%, final O₂ 16.1%, and an input fan sequence represented as “5 2 0 max.” A NASA operational note describes leading-edge blowoff and later loss of the remainder of the flame at maximum flow. That note must not be converted into the claim that blowoff occurred at the sequence’s starting 5 cm/s setting. The record does not independently establish every parameter used in the illustrative physics calculation, including exact run-level pressure or a measured numerical gravity.

C.  Microgravity-to-Earth comparison and principled refusal

Changing only gravity to approximately 10⁻⁶ g yields a PMMA rod fingerprint that can be evaluated, but the checked fixed-flow comparison to 1g returns NO_VALIDATED_BRIDGE for the proposed inverse equivalence. This is a model/constraint refusal, not missing NASA evidence. An oxygen 13.0% case with the remaining Earth-side input settings is outside the selected PMMA rod model’s supported oxygen scope and should return OUT_OF_DOMAIN_ABSTENTION without a fabricated outcome. These test cases demonstrate why record retrieval, fingerprint evaluation, and cross-gravity validation must be separately labeled.

B.  Risk and reproducibility register

  • Physics residual ≠ flame equivalence: preserve unmatched pressure, pO₂, chemistry, thermal radiation and material properties.
  • NASA evidence ≠ model training: curated condition records without verified outcome labels cannot support supervised fire-outcome predictions.
  • Low-n posterior: only 19 observations and three negatives make probabilities prior-sensitive and non-generalizable.
  • Data source disagreement: five conflicting gas fields are unresolved; never silently impute or override NASA sources.
  • Media segmentation: brightness/frame-difference screening is not adjudicated ignition, extinction, or spread-rate evidence.

Interface demonstration: do not mislabel schematic fire animation as real flame simulation, or condition similarity as experimental certainty.

  • Scope of deployment: the production site is a research prototype, not a certified fire-safety tool.

XIII.  Implementation Stack and Engineering Tools

The inspected Vercel project is a production READY FastAPI deployment. Its production requirements list Python FastAPI, Pydantic, ReportLab, Uvicorn, NumPy, SciPy and pandas. The dashboard comprises served HTML/CSS/JavaScript interactive views. Numerical routines include deterministic algebra, model routing, scoped optimization and posterior quadrature; source rendering and report/export features are integrated. Vercel provides public deployment and API hosting. Pre-recorded voice assets and cinematic presentation media are interface/presentation components, not scientific training evidence.

Source engineering tools: Python scientific stack for numerical computations and data preparation; source URLs and SHA-256 fingerprints for provenance; NASA PSI-25 and NASA NTRS for original scientific source documents; Vercel for deployment; JavaScript/CSS for frontend interaction. Do not assume every algorithm available in a recovered research-core package is externally validated and active in production merely because source code exists.

XIV.  Innovation, Benefits, and Expected Impact

EMBER’s distinct engineering value lies in linking four ordinarily disconnected tasks: (i) finding relevant ISS combustion experiments; (ii) retaining original metadata and provenance; (iii) interpreting a bounded material-specific equation; and (iv) visibly declining unsupported comparisons. Researchers, students and experiment planners can rapidly move from a query to NASA source records and a model-specific reasoning trail. In a spacecraft-safety setting, that traceability is a safer research communication pattern than a universal-looking black-box prediction. Future work should prioritize validated outcome extraction, model-domain review, human scientific adjudication, and source-versioned statistical testing over simply adding more AI models.

XV.  Conclusion

EMBER demonstrates a functioning evidence-centric engineering approach to microgravity combustion research. It organizes NASA BASS-II records with source-aware QA, applies selected published physical scaling relations through a six-adapter router, attempts constrained regime matching, distinguishes a small-sample Bayesian ignition reference from deterministic physics, and reports limits and abstention instead of unsupported certainty. Its current strength is reproducible, explainable scientific retrieval and analysis; neither the present data inventory nor numerical self-checks supports a claim of universal fire prediction or independent spacecraft safety certification.
